ig_caption:
One bad loss, then five more in an hour. That sudden cliff on your rating graph has a name: tilt.

It rarely looks like a slow decline. It looks like one evening. The signs are easy to spot once you know them: you start moving faster after a loss, you hit rematch straight away, and you play on long past the point you meant to stop.

The fixes are simple and dull, which is why they work: decide your stopping rule before the first game, take a proper break after a painful loss, and look at what went wrong before you queue again.

slides.title: That cliff on your graph?
slides.sub: HOW TO SPOT IT, HOW TO STOP IT

slides.title: A cliff, not a slope
slides.body: A real slump drifts down over weeks. Tilt is a sharp drop in a single session: one bad loss, then a string of quick ones, each played worse than the last.
slides.note: Find the steepest drop on your graph. Check what time it started.

slides.title: You start moving faster
slides.body: After a loss it's tempting to play quickly, to get to the next game. Moves made in a hurry are where the blunders come from.
slides.note: Look at your last losing streak. Did your moves get quicker as it went on?

slides.title: The rematch button
slides.body: Pressing rematch straight away to win the points back means the new game is really about the old one. You're playing your anger, not the position.
slides.note: If you want the points back badly, that's the moment to stop.

slides.title: Decide the stop first
slides.body: Set your rule before the first game, while you're calm: a number of games, or a number of losses in a row. Then keep it, however the evening goes.
slides.note: A rule made mid-tilt always says one more.

slides.title: Look before you queue
slides.body: After a painful loss, stand up for a few minutes. Then find the move where it went wrong before you start another game.
slides.note: One lesson from a loss is worth more than five quick games.

slides.title: Every cliff is on the poster.
slides.sub: Your whole rating history, on one print.
